item.title: China urges Japan to face history as war criminal enshrinement arrangement documents exposed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The documents proved once again that the Japanese government at the time knew full well the disgrace of enshrining Class-A war criminals and, fearful of the consequences, deliberately kept the decision-making process secret, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday.
Mao made the remarks at a regular news briefing when asked to comment on Japanese media's disclosure for the first time of internal meeting minutes of the Yasukuni Shrine, which revealed the decision-making process of the enshrinement of 14 Class-A war criminals including Hideki Tojo.
The documents show that the Japanese government made arrangements on the enshrinement of Class-A war criminals with the shrine in as early as the 1960s, but chose to keep the public in the dark until it was revealed in 1979.
These Class-A war criminals were the chief culprits behind Japanese militarists' war of aggression with the blood of innumerable war victims on their hands, Mao said, adding that the solemn verdict of the Tokyo Trials condemned them to perpetual infamy, thereby upholding international justice and laying the legal foundation for the postwar international order.
"Yet those running the Japanese government have again and again paid respects to what is in fact a shrine to war criminals. One has to ask: where has the conscience gone?" she said.
"History shall not be rewritten. Truth shall not be erased. Japan committed undeniable crimes during its militarist aggression. Those running the Japanese government must face history squarely, reflect on the war crimes, and make a genuine break with its militarist past," she said.

item.title: Xi's principles on settling Africa's hotspot issues resonate across continent
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
This photo taken on Jan. 23, 2025 shows locomotives waiting for maintenance outside the repair workshop of the Mombasa-Nairobi Railway in Nairobi, Kenya. (Xinhua/Wang Guansen)
NAIROBI, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The four principles proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping for resolving Africa's hotspot issues have resonated across the continent, with diplomats, scholars and media professionals hailing them as timely and practical guidance for promoting peace and development in Africa.
The four principles -- adhering to the principle of "Africa-led," upholding fairness and justice, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace, and addressing both symptoms and root causes -- were put forward on Tuesday in Beijing during Xi's meeting with Faure Essozimna Gnassingbe, president of the Council of Ministers of Togo, who is on an official visit to China.
Noting that the proposal comes at a time when conflicts across the continent are compounded by external interference and intensifying geopolitical rivalries, African experts said they support its emphasis on building lasting security through African ownership, international fairness, peaceful dialogue and sustainable development.
AFRICAN OWNERSHIP
At the heart of the four principles is the "Africa-led" approach, under which the African people are the true masters of Africa, and should play a central role in regional affairs.
Claudio Rabenja, a Malagasy economist and international affairs expert, said the principle is "relevant and particularly important in the current geopolitical context," as crises in Africa stem from complex local factors that outside actors often fail to understand.
"Solutions imported from or imposed by external actors do not always provide lasting answers," he said, adding that Xi's approach responds to Africa's aspiration to stop being a battleground for major-power rivalry and is consistent with China's tradition of non-interference.
Similarly, Etienne Bankuwiha, a Burundian sinologist, said Xi's proposal "consolidates the fundamental principle of African solutions to African problems," affirming that African countries are entitled to choose their own partners and development paths while rejecting externally imposed governance agendas.
Emmanuel Yenshu Vubo, dean of the Faculty of Social and Management Sciences at the University of Buea in Cameroon, said Africa "is not and cannot be reduced to mere spheres of influence or former colonial units that have only nominal independence ... Africa should be its own master."
A flight operated by China Southern Airlines arrives at Addis Ababa Bole International Airport in Addis Ababa, capital of Ethiopia, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Geng Xinning)
FAIRNESS AND JUSTICE
The principle of upholding fairness and justice calls on all parties to abide by the principles of the UN Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned.
Rabenja said respect for sovereignty and the UN Charter helps safeguard territorial integrity, curb destabilizing interventions and promote the peaceful settlement of disputes.
"It is essential that African countries be able to resolve their disputes without being subjected to pressure that runs counter to their national interests," he said, noting that China's consistent stance gives African governments greater freedom to make their own choices.
Gerard Njoya, editor-in-chief of Actu Chine Cameroon, said the principle reinforces the African Union (AU)'s Agenda 2063 by opposing unilateral sanctions and arbitrary interventions, addressing the long-standing demand for "an end to interference and double standards."
Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia, said the principle's call for consistent application of international law underscores the need to treat African countries fairly and with dignity.
PEACE THROUGH DIALOGUE
Noting that wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts, experts said the principle of promoting peace through a cessation of hostilities calls for mutual respect, extensive consultations, seeking common ground while setting aside differences, and fostering mutual understanding and accommodation.
Moutlakgola Masire, a journalist at Radio Botswana, said multi-stakeholder consultations and ceasefire commitments can prevent further civilian suffering and open the way for sustainable settlements.
Rabenja said military confrontation without a credible political process often fails to eliminate the root causes of violence.
"Mutual concessions do not mean abandoning fundamental principles," he said. "They recognize that lasting peace often requires arrangements acceptable to all parties."
China's diplomatic experience and relations with African countries can help support mediation, complementing the efforts of the AU, subregional organizations and the United Nations, he said.
Njoya said ending hostilities through dialogue aligns with the AU's Silencing the Guns initiative, offering an approach to conflict resolution rooted in African values.
Communication engineer Zhou Junbing (R) talks with a Kenyan train driver aboard a Mombasa-bound locomotive on the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) in Kenya, July 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Guang)
SECURITY AND DEVELOPMENT
As the principle of addressing both symptoms and root causes calls for tackling immediate security threats while pursuing long-term development, experts said China can help Africa address its challenges, citing its contributions to infrastructure construction, scholarships and vocational training across the continent.
Rabenja called security and development "two inseparable dimensions of stability."
Beyond protecting civilians in the short term, he said, the underlying causes of conflict -- poverty, youth unemployment, inequality and weak institutions -- must be addressed through investment in education, agriculture, energy, infrastructure and industrialization.
"Security creates the conditions necessary for investment, while development reduces some of the vulnerabilities that can fuel conflict," he said.
Njoya said addressing root causes is essential to achieving the goals of Agenda 2063, adding that the principle "endorses the AU's integrated approach, which seeks to tackle poverty, youth unemployment and inequality -- the underlying causes of instability."
Bankuwiha said China-Africa cooperation in agriculture, industrialization, poverty alleviation, green transition and infrastructure provides the economic empowerment needed to address the structural drivers of conflict in regions such as the Horn of Africa and the Lake Chad Basin.
Observers said the four principles forge "a new framework of equal partnership" that respects Africa's independent choices.
"Taken together, these four principles can serve as a practical reference guide for settling past, present and future hotspot issues in Africa," Demissie said.

item.title: Xi congratulates Hunan University on its centenary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday extended congratulations to faculty, students and alumni of Hunan University as it marks its 100th anniversary.
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a congratulatory letter to the university.
Xi urged the university to carry forward fine revolutionary traditions, continue to elevate the quality and levels of its teaching, and strive to nurture more talent who can apply their knowledge to practical affairs, so as to make new contributions to building China into an education powerhouse and advancing Chinese modernization.
Founded in 1926, Hunan University has nurtured a wealth of outstanding talent over the past century.

item.title: Long March legacy takes root in greener landscapes of revolutionary heartlands
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
This aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 4, 2026 shows a general view of Zhongfu Village in Changting County, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Photo by Zhu Fangbin/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Perched on a hillside in Changting County of southern China, visitors soak in lush scenery stretching beside the glistening Tingjiang River.
But things weren't always so picturesque.
Changting, an old revolutionary base area in Fujian Province, was among the counties hardest hit by soil erosion in China's red-soil region, which threatened local people's livelihoods and left the landscape degraded.
Efforts to improve the local environment began nearly a century ago.
In November 1931, the Communist Party of China (CPC) established the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic in Ruijin, Jiangxi Province, where the CPC put its revolutionary ideals into governance experimentation. The following year, it launched a tree-planting campaign to protect farmland from floods and droughts, reclaim barren hills and benefit local people.
During this campaign, CPC-led Red Army soldiers in Changting, which neighbors Ruijin, taught residents how to plant trees. In turn, residents brought food and seedlings to the soldiers and joined the planting campaign voluntarily.
"Even amid the turmoil of war, the Party still called for tree planting with great vigor," said Chen Liping, a researcher of CPC history and local chronicles in the county. "It reflects the Party's commitment to putting people's interests first and laying the foundations for future development."
As the war intensified, however, the tree-planting campaign had to be halted. The Red Army then embarked on the Long March, an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) forces. With some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers, the arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
As one of the starting points of the Long March, Changting has carried forward the Red Army's legacy in its decades-long efforts to combat soil erosion.
Tree planting, as the Red Army had practiced earlier, remained an effective method to tackle the problem. However, in severely eroded areas, ground temperatures can soar above 70 degrees Celsius, making it difficult for trees to survive.
Through experimentation, the county developed a phased approach suited to its natural conditions: first planting grass, then shrubs, and next trees, bringing the barren hills back to life step by step.
"Grass helps lower ground temperatures and create favorable conditions for other vegetation, allowing a mix of tree species to take root," said Shangguan Yuanbin, deputy head of the county's soil and water conservation station.
Over the years, local people adapted to changing conditions and met emerging problems with determination, patience and ingenuity.
Years of effort have paid off. To date, Changting has reduced the area affected by soil erosion by about 1.17 million mu (about 78,000 hectares), while its soil erosion rate fell from 31.47 percent to 6.31 percent, according to local authorities.
"Had we given up at any point over these decades, we would not have achieved such results today," said Shangguan. "We've applied the fearless Long March spirit to soil and water conservation."
Changting's transformation epitomizes a broader greening trend in China, which marks a national tree-planting day annually. Official data showed that between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation, while its forest and grass coverage rate exceeded 56 percent in 2025.
China's greening endeavor has gained international recognition. In 2021, Changting's comprehensive soil erosion control and ecological restoration practices were selected as a model case at the 15th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP15).
But restoring the land is not the end of the story. The next challenge is to turn environmental recovery into lasting economic opportunities for local communities.
One of these places is Xikuangshan, an old mining area in central China's Hunan Province. During the Long March, about 1,500 well-disciplined Red Army soldiers were stationed there for a week. Through their words and deeds, they gained the trust of locals, who went from hiding from the Red Army to following it.
Dubbed the "World's Capital of Antimony," Xikuangshan has witnessed decades of intensive underground mining dating back to 1897, which led to vegetation loss, air and water pollution, and ground subsidence. Some even joked that "a white bird flying across Xikuangshan could turn black."
In 2004, local people mounted an all-out campaign for ecological restoration. Inspired by the perseverance shown by the Red Army, a research team conducted countless experiments and finally achieved a breakthrough in the treatment of harmful residue generated during antimony refining, a challenge that has long confronted the industry worldwide.
The once-scarred mining landscape gradually regained its vitality. The improved environment, together with its revolutionary history and mining culture, helped Xikuangshan to develop into a well-known tourist destination with around 300 million yuan (about 44.6 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue annually.
Yang Lijun is among those who have benefited. After more than a decade, he decided to return home in 2021 upon seeing his hometown's blue skies and clear waters. He rented an abandoned rural house and opened a tourist restaurant featuring local specialties, which now generates an annual income of more than 100,000 yuan.
"In the past, many residents, myself included, left home because of worsening environmental conditions," he recalled. "Now, with the environment improving, more tourists are coming, bringing new opportunities for a better life."
For places like Changting and Xikuangshan, ecological restoration is therefore not simply about bringing back greenery, but also about higher-quality lives and new development paths for former revolutionary base areas.
Earlier this year, China issued guidelines on accelerating the development of such areas, with measures to support systematic environmental protection and encourage eco-tourism.
For Yue Hui, director of the soil and water conservation center in Changting, the changes are encouraging, but the work is far from over.
"Combating soil erosion requires sustained effort. We will continue our march toward a greener future," Yue said.

item.title: 70 years on, China's Canton Fair highlights innovation, intelligence in global trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Overseas buyers take photos outside the venue of the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
GUANGZHOU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 140th edition of the China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, opened to visitors in Guangzhou, capital of south China's Guangdong Province on Thursday, with more than 30,000 exhibiting companies and about 340,000 overseas buyers expected to attend.
Serving as a barometer and wind vane of China's foreign trade, this year's fair, marking its 70th anniversary, features innovation, intelligence, greater specialization and higher quality.
The Canton Fair is one of the world's few one-stop trade platforms offering a complete range of products with convenience and efficiency, while bringing together the latest products and technologies.
Overseas buyers communicate during the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
About 64 percent of exhibitors apply new technologies such as the industrial internet and artificial intelligence (AI). New and green products account for 23.2 percent and 26 percent of the exhibits, respectively, with both hitting record highs, and more than 700 new-product launch events will be held.
The fair has further enhanced its digital and intelligent operations, introducing 22 smart application scenarios and 16 AI applications for the first time, while booth navigation now covers the entire venue. "We have always worked together with exhibitors and buyers to jointly uphold the multilateral trading system and promote the building of an open world economy," said Zhu Yong, director of the China Foreign Trade Center.
The 140th Canton Fair runs in three phases in Guangzhou from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4.
Over the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has grown into China's largest and longest-running international trade event, with the most complete product range, the largest number of buyers and the highest transaction volume.

item.title: Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen named among FAO's 100 women heroes
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Yin Yuzhen attends a ceremony for Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' (FAO) 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, in Rome, Italy, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan)
FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu said women are a driving force in agrifood systems, playing an indispensable role in food security, natural resource management, rural development and community resilience.
ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen has been named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
The honorees were celebrated at a ceremony on Thursday at the FAO headquarters in Rome as part of this year's World Food Forum.
Yin has spent more than four decades combating desertification in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. After decades of persistent tree planting, she and her family have transformed stretches of the once-barren landscape into a green expanse, overcoming harsh conditions and shifting sands.
Her story also forged an enduring friendship with retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who raised 5,000 U.S. dollars decades ago to support her afforestation work.
Yin told Xinhua that the recognition had strengthened her resolve to continue her work. "Like a Mongolian horse, I will keep pressing forward with perseverance and determination, doing my work well and giving back to nature," she said.
Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen (2nd L, front) attends a ceremony in Rome, Italy, Oct. 15, 2026. Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was named on Thursday among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). (Xinhua/Li Jing)
Sitting in the audience, Sakolsky's eyes grew moist as he applauded Yin's achievement. "Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," he told Xinhua.
Addressing the ceremony, FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu hailed women farmers' roles. He said women are a driving force in agrifood systems, playing an indispensable role in food security, natural resource management, rural development and community resilience.
Qu then invited Sakolsky to join Yin on stage. The two friends embraced once again and held up a trophy together. Qu said that although Sakolsky was not among the women heroes, his "passion" and "solidarity" should be recognized.
Sakolsky expressed his gratitude, saying he was deeply moved by Yin's remarkable achievement. He called on everyone to plant a tree and work together to make a difference to the environment.
Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Qu Dongyu (L) presents the award to Dong Minfang during a ceremony for FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, in Rome, Italy, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan)
Launched by the FAO to mark the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026, the global initiative recognizes 100 women for their outstanding contributions to agriculture, food systems and rural development.
The FAO said it received 609 nominations from 131 members. The selection process involved an eligibility review, an assessment, and ranking by senior management, and two rounds of deliberations.
Besides Yin, Yu Jinxiu and Dong Minfang were also among the FAO 100 Women Heroes. Yu is a moxibustion therapist from Qichun County in central China's Hubei Province, and Dong is president of the Fengrui Agricultural Machinery Professional Cooperative in Yueyang County, central China's Hunan Province. They have spent years sharing their expertise to help thousands of people secure jobs and start businesses, raising incomes for rural residents.
The United Nations designated 2026 as the International Year of the Woman Farmer to highlight women's contribution to agrifood systems and promote policies and investments that improve their access to finance, knowledge and services.
Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Qu Dongyu (L) presents the award to Yu Jinxiu during a ceremony for FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, in Rome, Italy, Oct. 15, 2026. Yu is a moxibustion therapist from Qichun County in central China's Hubei Province. They have spent years sharing their expertise to help thousands of people secure jobs and start businesses, raising incomes for rural residents. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan)

item.title: Xi's article on advancing Party self-governance to be published
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance with higher standards and more concrete measures will be published on Friday.
The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 20th issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee.

item.description:

A flag-raising ceremony to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) was held at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing on Thursday.
